jurisdiction.name: Miami
jurisdiction.notes: City of Miami (Downtown, Brickell, Wynwood, Little Havana, etc.), zoned under the Miami 21 code, plus the Miami-Dade County items every city business needs. Florida restaurants are licensed by the state (DBPR), not county health. Miami Beach is a separate municipality with its own Certificate of Use, business tax receipt, 4% room / 2% F&B resort tax, alcohol hours and sidewalk-cafe rules, so treat these city-level entries as a guide only there and confirm with Miami Beach.

permits.name: Miami 21 zoning check for your use (before signing the lease)
permits.issuing_agency: City of Miami Office of Zoning
permits.notes: The City tells new businesses to confirm the property's transect zone and allowed uses (Miami 21, Article 4, Table 3) before signing a lease, because landlords often don't. Uses shown with a 'W' need an administrative Warrant and those with an 'E' need a public-hearing Exception. Meet with Zoning before any permitting or construction. A formal zoning verification letter is optional but useful for lenders and landlords.

permits.name: Building permit / change of occupancy (iBuild) with Certificate of Occupancy or Completion
permits.notes: All applications start electronically in iBuild/ePlan (ProjectDox). Plans route to building, zoning, fire, DERM and WASD reviewers. A change of use (e.g. retail to restaurant) ends in a Certificate of Occupancy, and a remodel ends in a Certificate of Completion. You can't apply for the Certificate of Use until construction is finished and the CO/CC is issued. Licensed subcontractors pull the plumbing, electrical and mechanical sub-permits, including the grease trap plumbing sub-permit.
permits.stall_risk: Multiple correction rounds across building, fire, DERM and WASD reviewers are the norm, and the CU clock can't start until the CO/CC is issued. Hire an architect with City of Miami restaurant experience and request the fire/life-safety expedited review where it is offered.

permits.name: Miami-Dade DERM environmental plan review (building permit, sewer capacity)
permits.issuing_agency: Miami-Dade RER – Division of Environmental Resources Management (DERM)
permits.notes: DERM reviews building permits, Certificates of Use/Occupancy and local business tax applications for air, solid waste, storage tank, pretreatment and sewer-capacity compliance. If the restaurant increases sanitary sewer flow, DERM issues a Sewer Capacity Certification Letter as part of plan review. Each review cycle runs about 24 hours to 10 business days. DERM also does an in-person inspection before final CU approval.

permits.name: Miami-Dade Water & Sewer (WASD) approval for change of use / new connection
permits.issuing_agency: Miami-Dade Water and Sewer Department – Utilities Development Services
permits.notes: WASD must evaluate and approve first-time connections, new construction, changes of use and most renovations. Restaurants usually increase water and sewer demand, so WASD checks whether the fronting sewer main can take the added flow. Start with a Utilities Information Request to confirm existing laterals and meters. Connection charges and any main extensions are invoiced separately.

permits.name: Occupant Load Certificate (places of assembly, 50+ occupants)
permits.issuing_agency: City of Miami Fire-Rescue – Fire Prevention Bureau
permits.notes: Restaurants, bars and clubs with 50+ people in a room need this certificate posted. You can't pass the CU fire inspection without it. Apply with an online pre-application, then upload City-approved plans with plumbing-fixture, building-occupancy and life-safety load tables, the dimensioned seating layout, and 44-inch egress paths in ProjectDox. Any deviation from the approved life-safety plan requires a new building permit.
permits.stall_risk: Seat layouts that don't match the permitted life-safety plan fail review and force a new building permit. Freeze the seating plan before the building permit is issued and submit the occupant-load package as soon as the CO/CC is final.

permits.name: Miami Fire-Rescue plan review, hood suppression and annual Fire Safety Permit
permits.issuing_agency: City of Miami Fire-Rescue – Fire Prevention Bureau
permits.notes: The Fire Prevention Bureau reviews construction plans (hood suppression, alarms, sprinklers, egress) and inspects every new business for its Certificate of Use. The annual Fire Safety Permit is then renewed with the CU invoice each September. Commercial cooking hoods need a licensed contractor to inspect the suppression system every six months, so keep the tags current. If you haven't heard back five business days after requesting the CU fire inspection, email FirePrevention@miamigov.com.

permits.name: City of Miami Certificate of Use (CU)
permits.issuing_agency: City of Miami Office of Zoning (with Fire, Code Enforcement and DERM inspections)
permits.notes: This is required before the City Business Tax Receipt and confirms the use is allowed at the address under Miami 21. Apply online with a $50 non-refundable fee. The City contacts you within five business days and then invoices Fire and Code Enforcement inspection fees. Once paid, schedule Fire and Code inspections via 311 and the DERM inspection, then get final zoning approval and post the CU. The CU expires each September 30 and the renewal invoice also covers the Fire Safety Permit.
permits.stall_risk: All inspections must pass within 90 working days of the application or you start over and pay again. The most common Code Enforcement failure is having no signed solid-waste hauler contract. Have the hauler contract, floor plan and occupant-load certificate ready before paying the CU invoice, and don't pay by check (14-day hold).

permits.name: City of Miami Business Tax Receipt (BTR)
permits.issuing_agency: City of Miami Finance Department – Business Tax Receipt section
permits.notes: Apply after the CU is issued, with a copy of the CU, your EIN and, for restaurants and hotels, the State of Florida DBPR license. After approval the City emails an invoice and then an interim BTR. A separate Miami-Dade County Local Business Tax Receipt is also required. Both renew for the October 1–September 30 fiscal year.

permits.name: Miami-Dade County Local Business Tax Receipt
permits.notes: Every business inside a Miami-Dade municipality needs both a city and a county receipt. Apply online through the Tax Collector's BTExpress, with your EIN and fictitious-name registration if you use a DBA. Eating establishments are taxed by seat count, roughly $45–$180 a year inside a city, but confirm the current category amount. Receipts run October 1 to September 30. Miami-Dade's tourist/restaurant tax registration asks for this account number.

permits.name: Miami-Dade DERM Grease Discharge Operating (FOG) permit
permits.issuing_agency: Miami-Dade RER – Division of Environmental Resources Management (DERM)
permits.notes: Any non-residential facility that prepares food and can discharge fats, oils or grease to the public sewer needs this annual permit (Chapter 24-42.6). Apply online after you have applied for the City CU. The permit is usually mailed within 30 days of approval, runs January 1–December 31, and can't be transferred, so new owners need their own. Only DERM-licensed haulers may pump the trap, and pump-outs are reported electronically each month.
permits.stall_risk: An undersized or missing grease trap means a plumbing sub-permit and construction before DERM signs off on the CU. Ask the landlord for the existing trap size and DERM permit history before signing, and get a FOG disclosure from the seller or lessor.

permits.name: Sign permit (Miami 21 Article 10)
permits.issuing_agency: City of Miami Building Department / Office of Zoning
permits.notes: Permanent signs are permitted through the Building Department (filed in iBuild) and must meet Miami 21 Article 10, Table 15 design standards for the property's transect zone. Illuminated signs also need an electrical sub-permit. In Wynwood (NRD-1) the Wynwood Design Review Committee weighs in, and warrant-level sign requests go through Planning. Unpermitted signs draw violation notices and fines.

permits.name: Sidewalk café permit (public right-of-way)
permits.issuing_agency: City of Miami Department of Resilience and Public Works
permits.notes: Pay the $175 non-refundable application fee and $10 inspection fee up front, then a security deposit by cashier's check at 444 SW 2nd Ave. The final permit fee is invoiced after Public Works, Planning, Zoning, Finance, Fire, Risk Management and NET all approve. You need the BTR, the CU, a survey under six months old, a scaled layout, furniture photos and liability insurance naming the City. On busy Brickell and Wynwood sidewalks, design for an ADA clear path, and add the outdoor area to any alcohol warrant if you will serve there.

permits.name: Alcohol reservation letter and liquor survey (distance separation)
permits.issuing_agency: City of Miami Office of Zoning
permits.notes: Alcohol service establishments submit a signed letter of intent and a signed-and-sealed liquor survey through ProjectDox. The survey shows the site meets City Code Chapter 4 distance separations from other licensed alcohol businesses, schools and churches, which are commonly cited as 1,500 / 1,000 / 300 ft, with many district exceptions. The state DABT application needs this local zoning sign-off.
permits.stall_risk: A distance conflict can make the site unlicensable for alcohol no matter how the build-out goes. Order the liquor survey during lease negotiation and make the lease contingent on the reservation letter.

permits.name: Miami 21 Warrant or Exception for alcohol service (bars, outdoor service, late hours)
permits.issuing_agency: City of Miami Planning Department / Planning, Zoning and Appeals Board (PZAB)
permits.notes: Where Miami 21 Table 3 doesn't allow the alcohol use by right, you need an administrative Warrant: staff review, certified-mail notice to neighbors, and a decision at least 30 days after notice, followed by a 15-day appeal window. Otherwise you need an Exception, which requires a PZAB public hearing ($1,500 fee plus $1,500 advertising, more if it goes to the City Commission). Both are valid for two years, during which you must obtain the CU. City Chapter 4 generally ends alcohol sales at 3 a.m. Police strictly enforce that in Wynwood, so later or 24-hour service needs specific approval in limited downtown areas. Miami Beach sets its own hours (2 a.m. for some South Beach venues).
permits.stall_risk: Exceptions wait for a PZAB hearing date, and anyone can appeal a Warrant or Exception within 15 days, which freezes it. Bars and late-night concepts should budget 3–6 months, line up neighborhood support before notices go out, and not assume hours past 3 a.m.

permits.name: Entertainment / nightclub use approval and noise compliance (Miami 21 + City noise ordinance)
permits.issuing_agency: City of Miami Planning Department / Office of Zoning
permits.notes: Live music, DJs and dancing turn a restaurant into an entertainment or nightclub use under Miami 21. Depending on the transect zone, the use must be allowed by right or approved by Warrant or Exception, and it must be reflected on your CU. The City's noise rules restrict amplified sound overnight (generally 11 p.m.–7 a.m.). Wynwood's NRD-1 pilot has allowed amplified music later on weekends, so confirm the current rule for your block. Outdoor speakers draw the most enforcement.

permits.name: Miami-Dade Convention & Tourist (bed) tax registration – hotels
permits.issuing_agency: Miami-Dade RER – Business Section (Convention and Tourist Taxes)
permits.notes: The county levies a 6% bed tax on stays of six months or less (3% convention development, 2% tourist development, 1% sports franchise) on top of state sales tax. Hotel restaurants also owe a 2% food & beverage tax. Register with the Tourist Tax Account Registration Form (needs your DOR, local business tax and DBPR numbers), then file monthly through TouristExpress by the 20th, even with $0 due. In Miami Beach the county 3% convention tax still applies but the city's 4% resort tax replaces the rest, and Surfside and Bal Harbour have their own.

permits.name: Miami-Dade 1% food & beverage (homeless & domestic violence) tax registration
permits.issuing_agency: Miami-Dade RER – Business Section (Convention and Tourist Taxes)
permits.notes: Non-hotel establishments with an on-premises alcohol license and more than $400,000 in annual gross receipts must collect a 1% tax on food and beverage sales. Register with the Food & Beverage Tax Account Registration Form once you expect to cross the threshold. Returns are monthly by the 20th, even when nothing is due. This doesn't apply in Miami Beach, Surfside or Bal Harbour.

permits.name: Florida DOH food service permit for bars without a kitchen (DOH-Miami-Dade)
permits.issuing_agency: Florida Department of Health in Miami-Dade County – Environmental Health
permits.notes: In Florida, county health departments permit only certain food operations: schools and institutions, civic and fraternal clubs, and bars and lounges that don't prepare time/temperature-controlled foods. Restaurants and bars with kitchens are licensed by DBPR instead. A drinks-only bar serving prepackaged snacks applies to DOH with Form DH 4086 and scaled plans (DH 8003 plan review). Once you add cooking, you move to DBPR.

permits.name: Food truck location rules (City of Miami Ch. 31) under state preemption
permits.issuing_agency: City of Miami Office of Zoning
permits.notes: Since 2020, state law (s. 509.102) has barred the City and County from requiring a separate food-truck license, permit or fee, so the DBPR MFDV license is your operating license. Local location rules still apply. The host property needs an active CU (up to two trucks, no more than three times a week, no overnight parking), and vacant land needs the owner's Temporary Use Permit. Three or more trucks count as a 'gathering' that needs a temporary event permit. The ordinance also bars trucks within 500 ft of food service or fuel establishments and in T3/T4-R zones, so check a site with Zoning before booking it.
